Summarise NEXUS's AI today in two sentences.

NEXUS's AI is a DeBERTa-based intent classifier that routes a sentence to the right module, plus hand-written parsers that turn some sentences into proposals you must confirm. It has no generative language model, no chat, and no generic tool system yet.

Is NEXUS an AI agent?

Not today. An agent would plan, call tools and verify results. NEXUS has a classifier and a propose-and-confirm action flow, which is much narrower. The Qwen roadmap aims toward agent-like behaviour in later phases.

How are the Qwen phases gated?

Each phase must pass its gate before the next starts: specification must be consistent, the dataset must pass validation, tool schemas and traces must validate, a training dry run must succeed, training must produce a loadable adapter, and evaluation must show useful agent behaviour. Integration happens only after that.

What AI does NEXUS have?
One model: a DeBERTa intent classifier that routes a sentence to the right module. There's no generative model.
So I can't ask it questions?
Not for written answers. You can ask, and it will tell you which area your request belongs to, or propose an action to confirm, but it can't compose an answer.
And that changes with Qwen?
That's the plan: Qwen3-8B would be the single generative model for conversation and reasoning. It's not trained or integrated yet, so today nothing changes.

Can I use my voice to create a task?
Partly. Your browser transcribes your speech, NEXUS classifies the text and can propose a task, but you still review and confirm before it's created.
Does my voice go to the cloud?
In Chrome and Edge, yes: the audio goes to the browser vendor for transcription. NEXUS itself only receives the text, and Firefox has no speech recognition.
Okay, I'll type it then.

What's the Qwen dataset phase?
Phase 2 of the roadmap: building and validating a training dataset of over ten thousand chat-format examples. It doesn't train anything or change NEXUS.
What's in it?

Twelve categories: general conversation, knowledge, reasoning, programming, maths, instruction following, assistant behaviour, NEXUS knowledge, tool-aware reasoning, capability boundaries, multi-turn context and safety.
Why include general stuff?
So the model stays broadly useful rather than becoming a NEXUS-only bot. The NEXUS and tool behaviour is added on top of general ability.

Is the classifier accurate?
It scored about 0.974 on its synthetic test set, but only 42 of 56 (75%) on hand-written natural-language requests.
Why the gap?
The test data was template-generated, so it resembled the training data closely. Real phrasing is messier, and some misses collapsed into risk_query.
Does the confidence threshold protect me?
Partly. The 0.90 threshold stops low-confidence routing, but some wrong predictions scored above it, so it's a guard, not a guarantee.
